articles.title: Brace for more foldable phones with this form factor (if readers get their way)

articles.body: It’s been over seven years since we first welcomed foldable phones to the market, and since then, they’ve taken on various forms. Some worked really well, like the mainline Galaxy Z Fold series , while others have fallen to the wayside, like Microsoft’s Surface Duo. While the latter is still regarded as a bad bet on Microsoft’s part — and is, arguably, more a dual-screen device than a foldable — it did seemingly predict one notable trend. This year, we’ve seen the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo adopt squatter form factors compared to devices before them, which raises the question: Do consumers prefer these short, squat screen aspect ratios over taller, narrower alternatives?

articles.title: Is Supabase secure? What it covers and what you have to cover
articles.excerpt: TL;DR. Yes, the platform is secure. Supabase is SOC 2 Type 2 and ISO 27001 certified, encrypts data at rest with AES-256 and in transit with TLS, and signs HIPAA agreements on the Team plan and above.…
articles.body: TL;DR. Yes, the platform is secure. Supabase is SOC 2 Type 2 and ISO 27001 certified, encrypts data at rest with AES-256 and in transit with TLS, and signs HIPAA agreements on the Team plan and above. Your project is a different question. Under Supabase's shared responsibility model, access to tables, API keys and auth settings are yours, and the platform does exactly what those settings say. On my local test table, one setting decided whether a public key got 0 rows or all 3. I'm Denys, a full-stack and AI engineer, and most apps I build or fix run on Supabase. People ask "is Supabase secure?" when they mean "is my data safe?". Those have different answers, so this article takes them one at a time. Is the Supabase platform secure? The platform side is audited by third parties.
articles.author: Denys Zaichenko

articles.title: Why agency leads go cold in 7 days and the 4-part follow-up system that fixes it
articles.excerpt: Most inbound leads don't die because the prospect chose a competitor. They go cold because nobody on your team owns the next touchpoint, or the conversation got buried in a personal WhatsApp thread or…
articles.body: Most inbound leads don't die because the prospect chose a competitor. They go cold because nobody on your team owns the next touchpoint, or the conversation got buried in a personal WhatsApp thread or inbox. In Indian agencies, especially those handling custom software, performance marketing, or design services, the first week determines everything. A prospect reaches out, has a good discovery call, and asks for a proposal. Your team starts building a deck or scope document. While you work on that internal output for three days, communication stops completely. By day seven, the prospect's internal urgency drops, or another firm simply stayed in touch better. The root cause isn't laziness. It's a lack of operational structure.
articles.author: Yashaswi Garg

articles.title: Why testing broken access control is still mostly a manual job — and what it takes to automate it
articles.excerpt: Broken object-level authorization has held the top spot on the OWASP API Security Top 10 for years now. It's also the class that scanners are worst at, for reasons that have less to do with tooling qu…
articles.body: Broken object-level authorization has held the top spot on the OWASP API Security Top 10 for years now. It's also the class that scanners are worst at, for reasons that have less to do with tooling quality than with what the vulnerability actually is. I want to lay out why, concretely, because "automate the login and replay the requests" sounds like a weekend project and turns out to be a state-machine problem. The bug isn't in the response — it's in the meaning of the response A scanner can tell you that an endpoint returned 200 and a JSON body. It cannot tell you whether that body should have been returned to this caller. GET /api/invoices/1234 returning a well-formed invoice document looks identical whether or not 1234 belongs to the authenticated user.

articles.title: Set up cex-uk-prices in 2 minutes, with a live check every week
articles.excerpt: cex-uk-prices looks up CeX UK's sell, cash and voucher prices from the same public search their website uses. Setup takes two minutes, because there's nothing to set up: git clone https://github.com/c…
articles.body: cex-uk-prices looks up CeX UK's sell, cash and voucher prices from the same public search their website uses. Setup takes two minutes, because there's nothing to set up: git clone https://github.com/casareanderson/cex-uk-prices && cd cex-uk-prices python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t . python3 -m cexuk "Sony WH-1000XM4" No packages, no key, no account. Testing something you don't control The risk with this one isn't my code, it's CeX. It's an undocumented endpoint, and it changes whenever their front end does. So the weekly check makes one real lookup from GitHub, as well as the offline tests: On 11 October that came back with 6 graded rows and £105 cash for the headphones. If CeX moves the search, that job goes red and I know before anyone opens an issue.

articles.title: Agent Feedback Loops and Parallel Agents: Two Books Read
articles.excerpt: I write reading notes on technical books. To check them, I have agents proofread them. An agent is one Claude instance, an AI working alone on a task with its tools. Each reviewer compares my claims t…
articles.body: I write reading notes on technical books. To check them, I have agents proofread them. An agent is one Claude instance, an AI working alone on a task with its tools. Each reviewer compares my claims to the book. One day, these reviewers flagged perfectly real facts as invented. The fault was mine: I had handed them condensed notes instead of the text of the book. They could not confirm what they could not see. A judge is only worth what it can see. Picture a student grading their own paper. They recognize their own ideas, find them clear, and give themselves a good mark. An outside grader sees what the student no longer can. (This image is mine, it does not come from the books.) With agents, this becomes a feedback loop.

articles.title: Cloudflare Counts 18.2 Million DDoS Attacks in Q3 2026, and 96% Ended Under Ten Minutes
articles.excerpt: TL;DR A distributed denial-of-service attack is a flood of traffic from many machines at once, aimed at exhausting a service's bandwidth, its connection table or its CPU until ordinary users stop gett…
articles.body: TL;DR A distributed denial-of-service attack is a flood of traffic from many machines at once, aimed at exhausting a service's bandwidth, its connection table or its CPU until ordinary users stop getting answers. Cloudflare published the 26th edition of its DDoS Threat Report on 29 October 2026, covering July, August and September 2026 across its own network. The quarter carried 18.2 million network-layer attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests, which works out at 8,226 network-layer attacks an hour, one every 0.44 seconds. Short-burst attacks under ten minutes and under 1 Gbps grew 208% year over year: 96% of network-layer attacks ended inside ten minutes, and 98% stayed under 1 Gbps.

I’ve always found Memories in Google Photos to be a useful and fun feature that often takes me back to the “good old days.” Whether it’s surfacing old clips of my friends and me from college or images from my first date with my wife, it’s usually great at showing the best moments of my life over the years. articles.title: Ancient star collisions could explain mysterious Little Red Dots and 'impossible' black holes
articles.excerpt: Collisions between stars in the early universe were common, and this could explain the growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Tele…
articles.body: New research suggests that collisions between stars in the early universe were common, which could help explain the rapid growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The team behind this research performed simulations of the early universe and found stellar systems were densely packed, leading to stars frequently slamming into each other. While rapid collisions would have destroyed the stars involved, slower collisions would have led to repeated mergers, creating single over-massive stars, which could collapse and form larger-than-usual black holes at the end of their lives. These could be the seeds of the first supermassive black holes.

articles.title: Voting in space: NASA astronauts cast ballots from International Space Station
articles.excerpt: The three Americans currently living off Earth made sure their voices were heard, voting in the midterm election from the International Space Station.
articles.body: The three Americans currently living off Earth just made sure their electoral voices were heard. Anil Menon told us today (Nov. 3) that he and fellow NASA astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins voted in the U.S. midterm elections from the International Space Station (ISS). "Yes, you can even vote from space! All three U.S. crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials," Menon wrote in an X post this morning . Yes, you can even vote from space! articles.title: 'OGame' developers explain how the browser-based sci-fi game has lasted 24 years ahead of the huge Orion update
articles.excerpt: The OG sci-fi browser game is still going strong.
articles.body: If you were on the Internet in the early 2000s looking for free browser games to play, OGame was a blooming sci-fi strategy sensation that couldn't be ignored. With online servers providing the structure for a living and evolving universe where players fought, traded, and created empires from scratch, its limited visual presentation was no issue. Times have changed, but GameForge hasn't gone anywhere. OGame has been ported to mobile devices, and content updates have kept it alive and fresh for much longer than a plethora of installable MMO games.

articles.title: Dimorphos in sight: Europe's Hera probe gets its 1st look at battered space rock (photo)
articles.excerpt: Europe's Hera planetary defense spacecraft is closing in on the binary asteroid system targeted by NASA's DART deflection test, and can now tell the two rocky bodies apart.
articles.body: Europe's Hera planetary defense spacecraft is closing in on the binary asteroid system targeted by NASA's DART deflection test, and can now tell the two rocky bodies apart. Hera is nearing the end of its voyage to the Didymos asteroid system, having launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in October 2024. The spacecraft snapped the image of Didymos and the smaller Dimorphos on Oct. 18 from a distance of 795 miles (1280 kilometers) from the pair, which are currently about 122 million miles (197 million km) from Earth. "With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," Michael Kueppers, Hera project scientist at the European Space Agency (ESA), said in a statement .
